evidence_quotes.quote: The seventh round was conducted in 34 African countries from 2016 to 2018, the most recent at the time of writing.

Our main outcome of interest is household access to water. To measure this, we utilize the following question from the Afrobarometer survey: “Over the past year, how often, if ever, have you or anyone in your family gone without enough clean water for home use?”
Of particular relevance to us is the question that asks about their history of paying bribes when trying to secure water, sanitation, or electric services from the government.
We are therefore careful to interpret this as a measure of utilities corruption rather than water corruption.

In Column 1, we estimate a probit model in which the dependent variable, Homesource, takes a value of one if the respondent's main source of water is in the house or the compound and zero if the source is outside the compound.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access and water source location across 34 African countries using Afrobarometer Round 7 household survey data.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), utilities-sector corruption and bribery paid to government officials to obtain utility services clearly qualify as governance/administrative factors, so plain_criterion2_decision is 'include'. Under the active 2026-10-13 A16 scope clarification, however, Criterion 2 requires a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership or regulatory structure). Here, the exposures are self-reported illegal bribery to obtain water, sanitation, or electric services pooled together and the regional average of that utilities-corruption indicator, analysed as general/sectoral corruption degrading infrastructure and technical service quality rather than any formal legal or administrative rule, eligibility requirement, tariff rule, regulatory regime, or ownership structure.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical study analyzing Afrobarometer Round 7 survey microdata (N = 44,778 respondents across 34 countries, 2016-2018) with probit, ordered probit, and mixed-effects regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water access availability/reliability (frequency of going without enough clean water for home use over the past year, coded both binary and 5-level ordered) and physical proximity/connection proxy (Homesource: main water source inside house, inside compound, or outside compound).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (individual/household respondents in 34 African countries, N = 44,778 in main access models and N = 44,546 in Homesource models), exposure (individual bribery for utilities and regional incidence of utilities corruption), outcome (household clean water access frequency and water source location), and study design (cross-sectional observational survey regression analysis) are clearly reported.

study_design: Cross-sectional observational household survey econometric study (probit, ordered probit, and mixed-effects regressions with country fixed effects and region-clustered standard errors)
country: 34 African countries (multi-country Afrobarometer Round 7 sample; examples named in text include Guinea and Mauritius)
population_and_sample: Representative samples of adult household respondents in 34 African countries from Afrobarometer Round 7 (2016-2018), N = 44,778 observations in main water access models (N = 44,546 in water source location models).
exposure: Regional incidence of utilities corruption (regional proportion of Afrobarometer respondents reporting paying a bribe, giving a gift, or doing a favor for a government official to get water, sanitation, or electric services) and individual household history of paying a bribe for utilities.
outcome: Household access to enough clean water for home use over the past year (binary indicator of anything other than 'always' going without water, plus 5-category ordered frequency) and location of main water source (inside house, inside compound, or outside compound).
rationale: This quantitative empirical study (Afrobarometer Round 7, N = 44,778 across 34 African countries) examines household water access outcomes (c1=yes, c3=yes, c4=yes, c5=yes, c6=yes), and would be included under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 because utilities-sector corruption and bribery are governance factors. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): its explanatory variables measure self-reported illegal bribery across pooled utility services (water, sanitation, or electricity) and regional utilities-corruption incidence as a governance/service-quality pathology, rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, formal administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, legal enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) governing water access.
